859:     /// Return every pin on every resident reserved for a shutdown handoff.
860:     /// A cell without an active request still gets one row, so a regular or
861:     /// outbound WebSocket cannot leave an otherwise empty stall invisible.
862:     pub fn drain_pins(&self) -> Vec<DrainPin> {
863:         let mut pins = Vec::new();
864:         for (cell, state) in self.cells.iter().filter(|(_, cell)| cell.quiescing) {
865:             let active: Vec<RequestId> = self
866:                 .active_requests
867:                 .iter()
868:                 .filter_map(|(request, request_cell)| (request_cell == cell).then_some(*request))
869:                 .collect();
870:             let regular_websocket_count = state
871:                 .websockets
872:                 .values()
873:                 .filter(|kind| matches!(kind, WebSocketKind::Regular))
874:                 .count();
875:             let outbound_websocket_count = state
876:                 .websockets
877:                 .values()
878:                 .filter(|kind| matches!(kind, WebSocketKind::Outbound))
879:                 .count();
880:             if active.is_empty() {
881:                 pins.push(DrainPin {
882:                     cell: cell.clone(),
883:                     request: None,
884:                     active_request_count: 0,
885:                     output_gate_count: 0,
886:                     regular_websocket_count,
887:                     outbound_websocket_count,
888:                 });
889:                 continue;
890:             }
891:             let active_request_count = active.len();
892:             for request in active {
893:                 pins.push(DrainPin {
894:                     cell: cell.clone(),
895:                     request: Some(request),
896:                     active_request_count,
897:                     output_gate_count: self

275:     /// Formats as `"<txid>/<checksum>"` — e.g. `"0000000000000001/8000000000000001"`.
276:     ///
277:     /// Ported from `Pos.String` in ltx@v0.5.1 ltx.go:102.
278:     fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
279:         write!(f, "{}/{:016x}", self.txid, self.post_apply_checksum)
280:     }
281: }
282: 
283: /// Parses a `Pos` from its canonical `"<txid>/<checksum>"` string form.
284: ///
285: /// The string must be exactly 33 characters: 16 hex digits, a slash, and
286: /// 16 hex digits.
287: ///
288: /// Ported from `ParsePos` in ltx@v0.5.1 ltx.go:80-99.
289: pub fn parse_pos(s: &str) -> Result<Pos> {
290:     if s.len() != 33 {
291:         return Err(Error::Other(
292:             format!("invalid formatted position length: {:?}", s).into(),
293:         ));
294:     }
295:     let txid = parse_txid(&s[..16])
296:         .map_err(|_| Error::Other(format!("invalid position txid: {:?}", &s[..16]).into()))?;
297:     // Validate that byte 16 is '/' (the separator) even though
298:     // Go's ParsePos (ltx@v0.5.1 ltx.go:80-99) blindly slices s[:16] and s[17:]
299:     // without checking the separator byte, so Go would accept e.g.
300:     // "0000000000000001X8000000000000001".  We keep the stricter check because:
301:     // (a) the '/' is mandated by the format doc and Pos.String() always emits it,
302:     // (b) silently accepting a malformed separator would hide caller bugs, and
303:     // (c) no production caller requires compatibility with the malformed form.
304:     // This is the conservative interpretation because it rejects bad input.
305:     if s.as_bytes()[16] != b'/' {
306:         return Err(Error::Other(
307:             format!("invalid formatted position (missing /): {:?}", s).into(),
308:         ));
309:     }
310:     // Same sign-prefix pre-validation as parse_txid: reject non-hex characters
311:     // so we match Go's strconv.ParseUint contract for the checksum field too.
312:     let checksum_str = &s[17..];
313:     if !checksum_str.bytes().all(|b| b.is_ascii_hexdigit()) {
314:         return Err(Error::Other(
315:             format!("invalid position checksum: {:?}", checksum_str).into(),
316:         ));
317:     }
318:     let checksum = u64::from_str_radix(checksum_str, 16).map_err(|_| {
319:         Error::Other(format!("invalid position checksum: {:?}", checksum_str).into())
320:     })?;
321:     Ok(Pos {
322:         txid,
323:         post_apply_checksum: checksum,
324:     })
325: }

327: // ── SQLite checksum ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
328: 
329: /// Computes a running SQLite WAL checksum over a byte slice.
330: ///
331: /// The slice length **must** be a multiple of 8 bytes (the function panics
332: /// otherwise, matching the `assert` in the Go source).
333: ///
334: /// `s0` / `s1` are the running checksum values (pass `(0, 0)` for the first
335: /// call, then thread the result through subsequent calls for incremental
336: /// checksumming).
337: ///
338: /// `big_endian` selects the byte order used to read 32-bit words from `b`:
339: /// `true` = big-endian (WAL headers with magic `0x377f0683`),
340: /// `false` = little-endian (WAL headers with magic `0x377f0682`).
341: ///
342: /// Ported from `Checksum` in litestream@v0.5.11 litestream.go:110-119.
343: ///
344: /// # Panics
345: /// Panics if `b.len() % 8 != 0`.
346: pub fn wal_checksum(big_endian: bool, s0: u32, s1: u32, b: &[u8]) -> (u32, u32) {
347:     assert!(b.len().is_multiple_of(8), "misaligned checksum byte slice");
348: 
349:     let mut s0 = s0;
350:     let mut s1 = s1;
351: 
352:     // Iterate over 8-byte units and compute checksum.
353:     // Matches litestream.go Checksum loop exactly.
354:     let mut i = 0usize;
355:     while i < b.len() {
356:         let w0 = if big_endian {
357:             u32::from_be_bytes([b[i], b[i + 1], b[i + 2], b[i + 3]])
358:         } else {
359:             u32::from_le_bytes([b[i], b[i + 1], b[i + 2], b[i + 3]])
360:         };
361:         let w1 = if big_endian {
362:             u32::from_be_bytes([b[i + 4], b[i + 5], b[i + 6], b[i + 7]])
363:         } else {
364:             u32::from_le_bytes([b[i + 4], b[i + 5], b[i + 6], b[i + 7]])
365:         };
366:         s0 = s0.wrapping_add(w0).wrapping_add(s1);
367:         s1 = s1.wrapping_add(w1).wrapping_add(s0);
368:         i += 8;
369:     }
370:     (s0, s1)
371: }

373: // ── Forward-slash path cleaning (Go stdlib `path`) ────────────────────────────
374: //
375: // The LTX path helpers below build object-store keys with Go's `path.Join`
376: // (NOT `filepath.Join`): the OS-independent, always-`/` package in
377: // `go/src/path/path.go`.  `path.Join` concatenates non-empty elements with a
378: // single `/` then runs the result through `path.Clean`, which collapses
379: // repeated separators, resolves `.`/`..`, and strips trailing slashes.  A
380: // naive `format!("{}/ltx", root)` skips this cleaning, so a root carrying a
381: // trailing slash (e.g. an S3 prefix `"backups/"`) would yield a DIFFERENT
382: // object key than the real binary (`"backups//ltx"` vs `"backups/ltx"`),
383: // breaking byte compatibility. We port `Clean`/`Join` byte-for-byte.
384: 
385: /// Lexically cleans a slash-separated path.
386: ///
387: /// A faithful port of `Clean` in the Go standard library `path` package
388: /// (`go/src/path/path.go`, `func Clean`).  It applies these rules iteratively
389: /// until no further processing is possible:
390: ///   1. Replace multiple slashes with a single slash.
391: ///   2. Eliminate each `.` path-name element (the current directory).
392: ///   3. Eliminate each inner `..` element along with the non-`..` element
393: ///      preceding it.
394: ///   4. Eliminate `..` elements that begin a rooted path (i.e. `/..` → `/`).
395: ///
396: /// The returned path ends in a slash only if it is the root `"/"`.  An empty
397: /// input returns `"."`.
398: ///
399: /// `pub(crate)` so `replica_url::clean_replica_url_path` can reuse Go's
400: /// `path.Clean` semantics rather than reimplementing them.
401: pub(crate) fn path_clean(path: &str) -> String {
402:     if path.is_empty() {
403:         return ".".to_string();
404:     }
405: 
406:     let bytes = path.as_bytes();
407:     let rooted = bytes[0] == b'/';
408:     let n = bytes.len();
409: 
410:     // Mirror Go's `lazybuf` with an explicit write cursor `w` over a fully
411:     // allocated buffer (we do not bother with Go's lazy aliasing optimisation,
412:     // but we DO preserve its cursor semantics, which the previous Vec-length
413:     // port got wrong).  `dotdot` marks the index below which `..` elements may
414:     // not backtrack.  The output is `buf[..w]`, so the byte at index `w` is the
415:     // next byte to be written — and is logically NOT part of the output yet.
416:     //
417:     // The backtrack loop must read `buf[w]` (the byte the cursor lands on),
418:     // NOT `buf[w-1]`: when it stops on a separator, that separator sits at
419:     // index `w` and is therefore EXCLUDED from `buf[..w]`.  A Vec-length model
420:     // that inspects `out.last()` (i.e. `buf[w-1]`) instead leaves the surviving
421:     // separator in the buffer, doubling it before the next element — the bug
422:     // this rewrite fixes.  See `go/src/path/path.go` `func Clean` / `lazybuf`.
423:     let mut buf: Vec<u8> = vec![0u8; n];
424:     let mut w = 0usize;
425:     let mut r = 0usize;
426:     let mut dotdot = 0usize;
427:     if rooted {
428:         buf[w] = b'/';
429:         w += 1;
430:         r = 1;
431:         dotdot = 1;
432:     }
433: 
434:     while r < n {
435:         if bytes[r] == b'/' {
436:             // empty path element
437:             r += 1;
438:         } else if bytes[r] == b'.' && (r + 1 == n || bytes[r + 1] == b'/') {
439:             // `.` element
440:             r += 1;
441:         } else if bytes[r] == b'.'
442:             && r + 1 < n
443:             && bytes[r + 1] == b'.'
444:             && (r + 2 == n || bytes[r + 2] == b'/')
445:         {
446:             // `..` element: remove to last `/`
447:             r += 2;
448:             if w > dotdot {
449:                 // can backtrack: step back over the just-ended element body,
450:                 // then keep stepping while the byte at the cursor is not '/'.
451:                 // When this stops on a '/', the cursor rests AT that '/', so it
452:                 // is excluded from `buf[..w]` (matching Go's `out.w` semantics).
453:                 w -= 1;
454:                 while w > dotdot && buf[w] != b'/' {
455:                     w -= 1;
456:                 }
457:             } else if !rooted {
458:                 // cannot backtrack, but not rooted, so append `..` element.
459:                 if w > 0 {
460:                     buf[w] = b'/';
461:                     w += 1;
462:                 }
463:                 buf[w] = b'.';
464:                 w += 1;
465:                 buf[w] = b'.';
466:                 w += 1;
467:                 dotdot = w;
468:             }
469:         } else {
470:             // real path element; add slash if needed
471:             if (rooted && w != 1) || (!rooted && w != 0) {
472:                 buf[w] = b'/';
473:                 w += 1;
474:             }
475:             // copy element
476:             while r < n && bytes[r] != b'/' {
477:                 buf[w] = bytes[r];
478:                 w += 1;
479:                 r += 1;
480:             }
481:         }
482:     }
483: 
484:     // Turn empty string into "."
485:     if w == 0 {
486:         return ".".to_string();
487:     }
488:     buf.truncate(w);
489:     // SAFETY-free: `buf` is built only from ASCII `/`, `.`, and bytes copied
490:     // verbatim from the valid-UTF-8 `path`, so it is always valid UTF-8.
491:     String::from_utf8(buf).expect("path_clean produced valid UTF-8")
492: }
493: 
494: /// Joins any number of path elements into a single slash-separated path,
495: /// cleaning the result.
496: ///
497: /// A faithful port of `Join` in the Go standard library `path` package
498: /// (`go/src/path/path.go`, `func Join`): empty elements are ignored, and the
499: /// joined string is passed through [`path_clean`].
500: fn path_join(elem: &[&str]) -> String {
501:     // Go returns "" when the total length of all elements is zero (which, since
502:     // empty elements are skipped, means every element is empty).
503:     if elem.iter().all(|e| e.is_empty()) {
504:         return String::new();
505:     }
506:     let mut buf = String::new();
507:     for &e in elem {
508:         if !buf.is_empty() || !e.is_empty() {
509:             if !buf.is_empty() {
510:                 buf.push('/');
511:             }
512:             buf.push_str(e);
513:         }
514:     }
515:     path_clean(&buf)
516: }
517: 
518: // ── LTX path helpers ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
519: //
520: // Ported from litestream@v0.5.11 litestream.go:184-197.
521: 
522: /// Returns the path to the LTX directory under a given root.
523: ///
524: /// Ported from `LTXDir` in litestream@v0.5.11 litestream.go:185:
525: /// `return path.Join(root, "ltx")`.
526: pub fn ltx_dir(root: &str) -> String {
527:     path_join(&[root, "ltx"])
528: }
529: 
530: /// Returns the path to the LTX level sub-directory.
531: ///
532: /// Ported from `LTXLevelDir` in litestream@v0.5.11 litestream.go:190-191:
533: /// `return path.Join(LTXDir(root), strconv.Itoa(level))`.  Note the
534: /// composition over the already-cleaned `LTXDir(root)`, which we preserve so
535: /// `..` resolution matches Go exactly.
536: pub fn ltx_level_dir(root: &str, level: u32) -> String {
537:     path_join(&[&ltx_dir(root), &level.to_string()])
538: }
539: 
540: /// Returns the path to a single LTX file for a given transaction range.
541: ///
542: /// The filename follows the convention `<minTXID>-<maxTXID>.ltx` with both
543: /// TXIDs formatted as 16-digit lowercase hex.
544: ///
545: /// Ported from `LTXFilePath` in litestream@v0.5.11 litestream.go:195-196:
546: /// `return path.Join(LTXLevelDir(root, level), ltx.FormatFilename(minTXID, maxTXID))`
547: /// and `FormatFilename` in ltx@v0.5.1 ltx.go:487
548: /// (`fmt.Sprintf("%s-%s.ltx", minTXID.String(), maxTXID.String())`).
549: pub fn ltx_file_path(root: &str, level: u32, min_txid: TXID, max_txid: TXID) -> String {
550:     let filename = format!("{}-{}.ltx", min_txid, max_txid);
551:     path_join(&[&ltx_level_dir(root, level), &filename])
552: }

77:     /// admission for a minute and a half while it walks down. Bounded
78:     /// concurrency is what makes the walk down finish in a time anyone can
79:     /// reason about.
80:     pub max_evictions: usize,
81:     /// Complete cell handoffs in flight at once during shutdown.
82:     ///
83:     /// `max_evictions` is tuned for a background walk down beside live
84:     /// traffic. This permit remains held through durability, release, and
85:     /// successor ownership acceptance. The successor's activation ceiling
86:     /// bounds the asynchronous restore wave after acceptance.
87:     pub max_releases: usize,
88:     /// Concurrent outbound WebSockets one cell may hold.
89:     ///
90:     /// Distinct from the node-wide pin budget, which counts *cells* held
91:     /// resident: one socket is enough to pin a cell, so that budget says
92:     /// nothing about how many a single cell may open. This bounds what one
93:     /// application can consume on its own behalf.
94:     pub max_outbound_websockets: usize,
95:     /// What an evicted cell's ownership record should say.
96:     ///
97:     /// Releasing it lets any node take the cell next, which is what makes a
98:     /// loaded node shed load rather than merely stop hosting it: keeping the
99:     /// record means every later request for that cell still routes here, to a
100:     /// node that already decided it has no room. Keeping it is right when the
101:     /// local eviction snapshot is the point, because a same-node wake is a
102:     /// rename instead of a restore.
103:     pub ownership_on_evict: OwnershipOnEvict,
104:     /// Production executors require a live self-node lease before serving.
105:     /// Deterministic unit slices which do not exercise node authority can
106:     /// disable this explicitly.
107:     pub require_node_lease: bool,
108:     /// Exact cross-node request protocol this process can authenticate and
109:     /// understand. A live owner speaking another version is unavailable, not
110:     /// stale: incompatibility never authorizes takeover.
111:     pub peer_protocol: u16,
112:     /// How long an activation effect may remain outstanding before the core
113:     /// stops waiting for it.
114:     ///
115:     /// Without this a swallowed effect is invisible: no event ever arrives, no
116:     /// timer is watching, and the request waits forever while every piece of
117:     /// state remains perfectly consistent. celld shipped that and parked
118:     /// requests past ninety seconds. `None` restores the old behaviour, which
119:     /// callers use only when they need to observe an indefinite wait.
120:     pub operation_deadline_ms: Option<u64>,
121:     /// How close an armed alarm may be before the cell stops being worth
122:     /// evicting. Inside this window the wake would cost more than the
123:     /// residency it saves, so the cell is held.
124:     pub alarm_resident_ms: u64,
125:     /// How long a cell may sit unused before the node gives it back, with no
126:     /// pressure involved. `None` keeps every cell resident until something
127:     /// needs the room.
128:     pub idle_evict_ms: Option<u64>,
129:     /// Ceilings and low watermarks for load shedding.
130:     ///
131:     /// `max_resident` is a hard cap on reservations; this is the softer,
132:     /// resource-aware question of whether the node is overloaded at all.
133:     /// Without it a node has only a cell count to reason about, so it meets
134:     /// memory exhaustion by running into it rather than shedding.
135:     pub pressure: pressure::PressureConfig,
136: }

316: /// Every way a cell's state can leave this process.
317: ///
318: /// This enum lists every external route. It is deliberately not
319: /// `#[non_exhaustive]`, so every exhaustive shell match stops compiling until
320: /// somebody decides how a new channel is held and how it is released.
321: ///
322: /// The core stores a channel and hands it back. It never reads it. A `match`
323: /// on `Channel` inside `celld-logic` would split one output invariant into a
324: /// separate rule for each channel.
325: ///
326: /// An alarm is missing here on purpose, and stays missing. Its consuming
327: /// commit does open a barrier -- as `GateOwner::Alarm`, keyed by the cell and
328: /// epoch the firing was dispatched against -- but a barrier is not a channel.
329: /// The alarm's settlement is not an egress: it is replayed back into the core
330: /// rather than released to the shell, it has no request to route by, and the
331: /// output gate does not release it to the shell, and it has no request to route
332: /// by. A variant here would force the core to match on `Channel` to tell a
333: /// release from a replay, which is the one thing this enum exists to prevent.
334: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)]
335: pub enum Channel {
336:     /// The answer to the cell event itself: an HTTP response, a cell RPC
337:     /// reply, or a peer-served reply.
338:     Response,
339:     /// `fetch()` from a handler to a third party.
340:     Fetch,
341:     /// A frame from a `webSocketMessage` handler, captured by the host and
342:     /// released from the cell's barrier queue.
343:     WsHibernatable,
344:     /// A frame on a socket the isolate opened and polls itself. It cannot be
345:     /// captured, because the handler may be awaiting the reply to the very
346:     /// frame being held, so it waits on a durability ticket instead.
347:     WsSelf,
348:     /// A service-binding call, `env.NAME.fetch()` or its RPC form.
349:     Service,
350:     /// A call to another cell: its `fetch` or one of its RPC methods.
351:     CellRpc,
352:     /// A leased Queue batch leaving its broker for a consumer Worker.
353:     Queue,
354: }
355: 
356: impl Channel {
357:     /// Return the diagnostic name for this channel.
358:     pub fn as_str(self) -> &'static str {
359:         match self {
360:             Channel::Response => "response",
361:             Channel::Fetch => "fetch",
362:             Channel::WsHibernatable => "ws_hibernatable",
363:             Channel::WsSelf => "ws_self",
364:             Channel::Service => "service",
365:             Channel::CellRpc => "cellrpc",
366:             Channel::Queue => "queue",
367:         }
368:     }
369: }

673:     ///
674:     /// The core never reads a clock or a proc file; the shell measures and
675:     /// hands the numbers over, and every decision that follows -- whether the
676:     /// node is overloaded, whether the latch stays hot, how far to shed --
677:     /// happens here where a schedule can replay it.
678:     LoadSampled {
679:         load: pressure::Load,
680:         now_mono_ms: u64,
681:     },
682:     /// Retire an exact cached remote route after a dispatch failure which is
683:     /// known not to have executed the request. Newer route generations are
684:     /// unaffected by delayed failure reports.
685:     InvalidateRemote {
686:         cell: CellId,
687:         node: NodeId,
688:         epoch: Epoch,
689:     },
690:     NodeFenced,
691:     /// The node is shutting down: release every resident cell and wait for a
692:     /// successor to publish it. Unlike an on-demand evict this always
693:     /// releases, whatever `ownership_on_evict` is set to. Complete handoffs
694:     /// run at most `max_releases` at a time, and a cell that is active when
695:     /// the drain begins is picked up once its activity finishes.
696:     ReleaseAll,
697: }
698: 
699: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
700: pub enum Route {

702:     Remote {
703:         node: NodeId,
704:         addr: String,
705:         epoch: Epoch,
706:         peer_protocol: u16,
707:     },
708: }
709: 
710: /// Exact resident isolate reserved for a top-level Worker request.
711: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
712: pub struct WorkerRoute {

714:     pub epoch: Epoch,
715:     /// A pending durability proof made stale by selecting this still-routable
716:     /// resident. The executor uses the ID only to release its effect waiter;
717:     /// a late completion is ignored by the core's phase check.
718:     pub retired_durability: Option<OpId>,
719: }
720: 
721: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
722: pub enum RequestError {
723:     NodeUnavailable,
724:     ResolveFailed,
725:     AcquireFailed,
726:     RestoreFailed,
727:     RuntimeFailed,
728:     PublishFailed,
729:     NodeFenced,
730:     PeerIncompatible,
731:     CapacityExhausted,
732:     /// A local write ran but its durability could not be proven, so the
733:     /// response must fail rather than falsely acknowledge the write.

735: }
736: 
737: /// Work performed outside the core. Every asynchronous effect is versioned;
738: /// completion events with an obsolete `op` are ignored.
739: #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
740: pub enum Effect {
741:     ScheduleTimer {
742:         timer: Timer,
743:         at_mono_ms: u64,
744:     },

747:     },

751:         record: NodeLeaseRecord,

753:         /// uses it to report how much authority remained when the attempt
754:         /// completed. An initial acquisition has no prior authority.
755:         authority_expires_ms: Option<u64>,
756:     },
757:     /// Read the local cell inventory. This is emitted only after the initial
758:     /// node lease CAS replaced the exact certified predecessor generation.
759:     ReadLocalCells,
760:     ReadOwner {
761:         op: OpId,
762:         cell: CellId,
763:     },
764:     ReadNodeLease {
765:         op: OpId,
766:         cell: CellId,
767:         owner: NodeId,
768:     },
769:     /// The takeover interlock, as a core decision (lease-fold): the dead
770:     /// owner's folded log state was not sealed, so its acked tail may
771:     /// exist only on its followers. The executor recovers every
772:     /// non-sealed session of `owner` into the bucket and reports
773:     /// `NodeLogRecovered`; only then does the claim proceed.
774:     RecoverNodeLog {
775:         op: OpId,
776:         cell: CellId,
777:         owner: NodeId,
778:     },
779:     /// Enumerate recent node leases and return their advisory load records.
780:     /// Listing and bounded parallel reads are adapter mechanics; selection,
781:     /// reservations, and exclusions are deterministic core policy.
782:     ReadCapacityPeers {
783:         op: OpId,
784:         cell: CellId,
785:     },
786:     CasOwner {
787:         op: OpId,
788:         cell: CellId,
789:         guard: CasGuard,
790:         epoch: Epoch,
791:         takeover: bool,
792:     },
793:     /// Bring the bucket's wake entry for this cell into line with its alarm.
794:     ///
795:     /// Emitted wherever the alarm settles, which is the only place that
796:     /// knows. An arm needs an entry; a consumed alarm needs its entry gone,
797:     /// or every later due scan finds a hint for an alarm that already fired

800:     ReconcileWakeEntry {
801:         cell: CellId,
802:         next_alarm_ms: i64,
803:     },
804:     /// Publish an evicted cell as unowned, keeping its epoch, so the next
805:     /// node to want it can take it without waiting for this one to notice.
806:     ReleaseOwner {
807:         op: OpId,
808:         cell: CellId,
809:         epoch: Epoch,
810:     },
811:     /// Ask a compatible peer to acquire a cell whose owner record was just

813:     /// restore and runtime publication continue outside the donor's shutdown
814:     /// critical path.
815:     AdoptReleased {
816:         op: OpId,
817:         cell: CellId,
818:         released_epoch: Epoch,
819:     },
820:     /// Interrupt the activity which existed when a cell entered its shutdown
821:     /// handoff batch. The shell maps core request IDs to handler/body aborts
822:     /// and closes sockets with a restart status.
823:     CancelCellActivity {
824:         cell: CellId,
825:         requests: Vec<RequestId>,
826:         websockets: Vec<WebSocketId>,

828:         /// sockets, and the cell stays on this node: its hibernatable sockets

830:         /// socket and forgets the pair, because the cell is leaving.
831:         keep_hibernatable: bool,
832:     },
833:     Restore {

835:         cell: CellId,
836:         spec: RestoreSpec,
837:     },
838:     StartRuntime {

840:         cell: CellId,
841:         epoch: Epoch,
842:     },
843:     Publish {
844:         op: OpId,
845:         cell: CellId,
846:         epoch: Epoch,
847:     },
848:     /// Prove that every commit made before this effect is recoverable from
849:     /// replica authority. Voluntary eviction cannot begin until this succeeds.
850:     EnsureDurable {
851:         op: OpId,
852:         cell: CellId,
853:         epoch: Epoch,
854:     },
855:     /// The output gate: prove the cell's committed `position` is replicated so
856:     /// a withheld local write response can be released. Unlike
857:     /// [`Effect::EnsureDurable`] this is per-request and changes no cell phase,
858:     /// so the cell keeps serving co-resident requests while one response waits.
859:     AwaitDurable {
860:         op: OpId,
861:         cell: CellId,
862:         epoch: Epoch,
863:         position: u64,
864:     },

866:     /// still names this node at this epoch. The core holds the gated write
867:     /// until `Event::OwnershipVerified` returns. Fleet-proof acks never
868:     /// emit this — the ensemble seal is their fence.
869:     VerifyOwnership {
870:         op: OpId,
871:         cell: CellId,
872:         epoch: Epoch,
873:     },
874:     StopRuntime {
875:         op: OpId,
876:         cell: CellId,
877:         epoch: Epoch,

879:     },
880:     FireAlarm {
881:         op: OpId,
882:         cell: CellId,
883:         epoch: Epoch,
884:         scheduled_ms: i64,
885:     },
886:     Complete {
887:         request: RequestId,
888:         result: Result<Route, RequestError>,
889:     },
890:     /// Release a withheld output now that the writes it can reveal are
891:     /// decided: `Ok` lets it leave, `Err` refuses it. Emitted only for an
892:     /// output the shell held open via [`Event::Output`].
893:     ///
894:     /// `channel` is the one the shell supplied, returned unchanged. It selects
895:     /// which adapter holds this effect and is the only thing the shell needs
896:     /// in order to route the release. No operation id rides along: the shell
897:     /// never learns the one the core assigned, and `(request, channel)` is
898:     /// unique by construction — `State::validate` enforces it.
899:     Release {
900:         request: RequestId,
901:         channel: Channel,
902:         result: Result<(), RequestError>,
903:     },

905:     /// the executor must use the ordinary stateless Worker pool.
906:     CompleteWorker {
907:         request: RequestId,
908:         route: Option<WorkerRoute>,
909:     },

911:     /// the cell carries on without it.

926:     pub epoch: Epoch,
927: }

933:     /// ownership record is released and the local replica is not worth
934:     /// keeping. An idle eviction is the opposite on both counts -- it
935:     /// keeps the record so the next activation here renames the file into
936:     /// place instead of paying a full remote restore.
937:     Evict {

940:     Fence,

944:     /// divergence, not the failure. Stop, keep no local snapshot, and let the

<content>
1: # What celld guarantees
2: 
3: celld makes two promises about your data. Exactly one node serves a cell
4: at a time, so two machines never write the same database. And celld does
5: not answer a write until that write survives a failure, so nothing you
6: were told succeeded is lost.
7: 
8: This page is how both promises are kept. Fencing is the part that keeps
9: the first one true when a node is slow, paused, or cut off from the
10: network: celld refuses that node's writes rather than trusting it to
11: notice it lost the cell. Both claims rest on the object
12: store, so this page starts with what you must provide: a bucket with
13: working conditional writes, and a supervisor that restarts the process.
14: The mechanism follows, so you can check the argument against the code.
15: 
16: ## What the bucket must provide
17: 
18: celld needs three properties from the object store:
19: 
20: - A conditional create: the write must fail when the object exists.
21: - A conditional overwrite: the write must fail when the object changed
22:   after the read.
23: - Read-after-write consistency: a read after a successful write must
24:   return that write.
25: 
26: The qualified stores are Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Tigris, Google Cloud
27: Storage, and Azure Blob Storage. celld's release tests run against R2,
28: and the S3 path uses the same client and the same headers.
29: 
30: Backblaze B2, Hetzner Object Storage, and DigitalOcean Spaces do not
31: implement the required conditional writes. celld is not correct on such
32: a store: two nodes can then own one cell. A store can also accept the
33: conditional headers and ignore the condition, and that store fails late
34: and silently — so run the storage test below.
35: 
36: MinIO (the community edition) implements the conditional writes and
37: passes the storage test, but celld has not qualified it for production.
38: One release is broken: RELEASE.2025-09-06T17-38-46Z answers the
39: conditional create of an absent object with `NoSuchKey`, so the first
40: deploy fails (denoland/celld#162). Use RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z or
41: later.
42: 
43: The request dialect differs per provider. An S3-compatible bucket gets
44: the `If-None-Match: *` and `If-Match` headers, and the condition
45: compares the etag. A `gs://` bucket selects the Cloud Storage XML API
46: with the `x-goog-if-generation-match` precondition and OAuth
47: credentials, because Cloud Storage does not apply `If-Match` to a PUT.
48: An `az://` bucket (the NAME is the container) uses the same `If-`
49: headers, which Put Blob applies. The adapter treats `AlreadyExists` and
50: `Precondition` (HTTP 412 on Azure) as clean conditional-write
51: rejections and keeps every other error ambiguous, because an ambiguous
52: write can have changed the object.
53: 
54: Azure was qualified on 2026-08-18 under an account key, a VM managed
55: identity, and an AKS workload identity, single-node. A managed identity
56: on Azure App Service or Azure Container Apps does not work; see
57: [limitations](limitations.md).
58: 
59: ## The storage test
60: 
61: No store publishes these properties, so celld asks the store directly.
62: The command `celld diagnose` sends four conditional writes to your
63: bucket and reports the result:
64: 
65: ```
66: ok bucket conditional write (create, reject-create, update, reject-stale)
67: ```
68: 
69: Two of the four writes must fail. A store that accepts either one
70: cannot fence a cell, so celld names the store as the fault and the
71: command exits with an error. Each node repeats the test once at
72: startup, and a node that finds a broken store stops. Set
73: `CELLD_STORAGE_PROBE=0` to disable the startup test, or run
74: `celld diagnose --read-only` with a credential that cannot write.
75: 
76: The test writes and deletes one small object under `probe/`. A process
77: that stops mid-test can leave the object behind; it is small, and celld
78: never reads it. celld reserves `probe/` together with `cells/`,
79: `nodes/`, `node-cells/`, `fleet/`, `deploy/`, `deploy-blobs/`, `wake/`,
80: and `telemetry/`, and it deletes objects under some of them, so an
81: application must not write under any of these prefixes.
82: 
83: celld does not require a ranged read today, so a store that ignores the
84: `Range` header can still run a fleet.
85: 
86: ## The supervisor
87: 
88: You must run celld under a supervisor that restarts the process, such
89: as systemd, Docker with a restart policy, or Kubernetes. A node fences
90: itself when it loses its lease (the mechanism is below), and a fenced
91: process exits; without a restart, the fleet loses that capacity until
92: an operator intervenes.
93: 
94: The supervisor must restart without an attempt limit, and it must wait
95: at least one lease lifetime between attempts. A node that cannot
96: acquire a lease at startup retries and does not exit, so a repeated
97: fence needs a node that acquires a lease and then loses it, and the
98: wait keeps that cycle slow enough to observe.
99: 
100: ## The mechanism
101: 
102: The short version: the ownership records use conditional writes, so two
103: nodes cannot acquire one cell. The replicated data carries its fencing
104: epoch in the object key, so a node that lost ownership writes only into
105: a superseded prefix. And before celld acknowledges a write, it proves
106: the write durable and confirms that it still owns the cell.
107: 
108: ### The ownership record
109: 
110: Each cell has one ownership record in the bucket. The record names the
111: owner node's session and carries a fencing epoch. A node acquires a
112: cell with a conditional write — a create when no record exists, a
113: compare-and-swap on the previous record when one does — and the bucket
114: accepts one such write, so two nodes cannot acquire the same cell.
115: 
116: Every activation advances the epoch, a takeover and a local wake alike.
117: Each owner therefore replicates under a fresh epoch, and an epoch never
118: has two writers.
119: 
120: ### The epoch prefix
121: 
122: The replicator copies each cell's SQLite data to the bucket under
123: `cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, with plain unconditional PUTs. The epoch
124: in the key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing,
125: but its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the
126: current lineage. (The tiering path can first combine segments from many
127: cells into a node bundle, and it drains each segment into its per-cell
128: prefix later.)
129: 
130: The prefix protects the new owner's data from stale writes. The next
131: two sections protect the durability promise.
132: 
133: ### The acknowledgement rule (RPO=0)
134: 
135: A gate holds each write response until a durability proof covers the
136: write. After a bucket proof, celld reads the ownership record once and
137: acknowledges only if the record still names this node at this epoch. A
138: partitioned node can commit locally and replicate into its superseded
139: prefix, but the ownership read then shows the new owner, so celld does
140: not acknowledge the write. The check reads the record instead of
141: comparing a clock, so a paused process or a skewed clock cannot pass
142: it.
143: 
144: A fleet proof does not require this read. The owner sends each write to
145: one or two other nodes, which hold a copy of its recent writes; those
146: nodes are its followers, and the set of them is the ensemble. Every
147: follower must fsync the write, and a takeover seals the prior node-log
148: session before it restores, so the stale owner cannot complete another
149: fleet proof.
150: 
151: ### The ensemble needs two nodes
152: 
153: A node picks its followers from the other nodes in the fleet, so it never
154: counts itself. One follower is enough, therefore a fleet needs two
155: running celld nodes before any node can complete a fleet proof.
156: `CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet` is the default, so a fleet of one node requests the
157: fleet posture and does not get it.
158: 
159: A node recruits up to two followers, so a fleet of three or more nodes holds
160: three copies of an acknowledged write. The ensemble keeps acknowledging while
161: one follower remains, therefore a fleet does not fall back to the bucket each
162: time it loses a follower.
163: 
164: A node without an ensemble stays correct. It acknowledges each write on a
165: bucket proof instead, so celld still does not acknowledge a write before a
166: durability proof covers it. The cost is latency: the write waits for the object
167: store, and an object store round trip is much slower than a follower fsync.
168: 
169: ### The takeover recovery gate
170: 
171: The default fleet mode can acknowledge a write once the node-log
172: ensemble stores it; the bucket upload can complete later. Each process
173: session therefore creates a conditional node-log record before its
174: first fleet-durable acknowledgement.
175: 
176: A cold activation checks the prior owner's log records before it reads
177: the bucket. An absent record proves that the session never acknowledged
178: past the bucket, and a sealed record proves that recovery completed. An
179: open or recovering record makes the activation run recovery: it fences
180: the record with a compare-and-swap, seals the reachable followers,
181: uploads their retained segments and bundles into the per-cell prefixes,
182: and then marks the record sealed. The activation cannot restore until
183: this sequence completes.
184: 
185: ### Full-prefix restore
186: 
187: A restore selects the newest epoch prefix that contains LTX data, and
188: it reads the full contiguous chain from transaction zero. celld no
189: longer writes an epoch seal object, and a legacy `e<epoch>.seal.json`
190: object does not limit the chain.
191: 
192: A fenced node can append an unacknowledged tail to an older prefix, and
193: a later restore can expose that tail. This does not violate the
194: contract, because a failed or absent acknowledgement does not prove
195: that the write is absent. The rule reads the full chain because a
196: node-log recovery or a bundle drain can add an acknowledged tail after
197: an earlier restore; a restore that stopped at the earlier cut would
198: hide that tail and lose acknowledged data.
199: 
200: ### Self-fencing
201: 
202: Each node holds a lease in the bucket. The lease carries an expiry, and
203: the node renews it after one third of the lifetime (`CELLD_TTL_MS`,
204: default 10000 ms). A renewal that does not reach the bucket does not
205: fence the node, because the node retries while the published expiry has
206: not passed.
207: 
208: A node that cannot reach the bucket cannot renew and cannot replicate,
209: so it must not own cells. When its published expiry passes, it fences
210: itself: it stops each active cell, and it fails every request that it
211: has not completed. A node whose lease record another writer replaced or
212: removed fences at once, because that record proves the authority moved.
213: 
214: The fence writes nothing to the bucket. Each peer already reads the
215: lease as dead or replaced, so a peer can acquire the cells through the
216: ownership records. And a request is safe even before the fence runs,
217: because celld compares the current time against the published expiry
218: each time it routes a request.
219: 
220: A fenced node logs a line that starts with `SELF-FENCE:` and stops with
221: the exit code 3. celld reports other internal failures with the same
222: prefix and code, so the line names the cause. The fenced state is
223: terminal: only a restart returns the node to the fleet, through the
224: same cold-activation path that a peer failure uses.
225: 
226: The failure of a node is a normal input, not a recovery procedure; the
227: [testing page](testing.md) shows the kill tests that exercise this
228: path.

(End of file - total 228 lines)
</content>

conditional create of an absent object with `NoSuchKey`, so the first
deploy fails (denoland/celld#162). Use RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z or
later.

The request dialect differs per provider. An S3-compatible bucket gets
the `If-None-Match: *` and `If-Match` headers, and the condition
compares the etag. A `gs://` bucket selects the Cloud Storage XML API
with the `x-goog-if-generation-match` precondition and OAuth
credentials, because Cloud Storage does not apply `If-Match` to a PUT.
An `az://` bucket (the NAME is the container) uses the same `If-`
headers, which Put Blob applies. The adapter treats `AlreadyExists` and
`Precondition` (HTTP 412 on Azure) as clean conditional-write
rejections and keeps every other error ambiguous, because an ambiguous
write can have changed the object.

Azure was qualified on 2026-08-18 under an account key, a VM managed
identity, and an AKS workload identity, single-node. A managed identity
on Azure App Service or Azure Container Apps does not work; see
[limitations](limitations.md).

## The storage test

No store publishes these properties, so celld asks the store directly.
The command `celld diagnose` sends four conditional writes to your
bucket and reports the result:

```
ok bucket conditional write (create, reject-create, update, reject-stale)
```

Two of the four writes must fail. A store that accepts either one
cannot fence a cell, so celld names the store as the fault and the
command exits with an error. Each node repeats the test once at
startup, and a node that finds a broken store stops. Set
`CELLD_STORAGE_PROBE=0` to disable the startup test, or run
`celld diagnose --read-only` with a credential that cannot write.

The test writes and deletes one small object under `probe/`. A process
that stops mid-test can leave the object behind; it is small, and celld
never reads it. celld reserves `probe/` together with `cells/`,
`nodes/`, `node-cells/`, `fleet/`, `deploy/`, `deploy-blobs/`, `wake/`,
and `telemetry/`, and it deletes objects under some of them, so an
application must not write under any of these prefixes.

celld does not require a ranged read today, so a store that ignores the
`Range` header can still run a fleet.

## The supervisor

You must run celld under a supervisor that restarts the process, such
as systemd, Docker with a restart policy, or Kubernetes. A node fences
itself when it loses its lease (the mechanism is below), and a fenced
process exits; without a restart, the fleet loses that capacity until
an operator intervenes.

The supervisor must restart without an attempt limit, and it must wait
at least one lease lifetime between attempts. A node that cannot
acquire a lease at startup retries and does not exit, so a repeated
fence needs a node that acquires a lease and then loses it, and the
wait keeps that cycle slow enough to observe.

## The mechanism

The short version: the ownership records use conditional writes, so two
nodes cannot acquire one cell. The replicated data carries its fencing
epoch in the object key, so a node that lost ownership writes only into
a superseded prefix. And before celld acknowledges a write, it proves
the write durable and confirms that it still owns the cell.

### The ownership record

Each cell has one ownership record in the bucket. The record names the
owner node's session and carries a fencing epoch. A node acquires a
cell with a conditional write — a create when no record exists, a
compare-and-swap on the previous record when one does — and the bucket
accepts one such write, so two nodes cannot acquire the same cell.

Every activation advances the epoch, a takeover and a local wake alike.
Each owner therefore replicates under a fresh epoch, and an epoch never
has two writers.

### The epoch prefix

The replicator copies each cell's SQLite data to the bucket under
`cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, with plain unconditional PUTs. The epoch
in the key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing,
but its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the
current lineage. (The tiering path can first combine segments from many
cells into a node bundle, and it drains each segment into its per-cell
prefix later.)

The prefix protects the new owner's data from stale writes. The next
two sections protect the durability promise.

### The acknowledgement rule (RPO=0)

A gate holds each write response until a durability proof covers the
write. After a bucket proof, celld reads the ownership record once and
acknowledges only if the record still names this node at this epoch. A
partitioned node can commit locally and replicate into its superseded
prefix, but the ownership read then shows the new owner, so celld does
not acknowledge the write. The check reads the record instead of
comparing a clock, so a paused process or a skewed clock cannot pass
it.

A fleet proof does not require this read. The owner sends each write to
one or two other nodes, which hold a copy of its recent writes; those
nodes are its followers, and the set of them is the ensemble. Every
follower must fsync the write, and a takeover seals the prior node-log
session before it restores, so the stale owner cannot complete another
fleet proof.

### The ensemble needs two nodes

A node picks its followers from the other nodes in the fleet, so it never
counts itself. One follower is enough, therefore a fleet needs two
running celld nodes before any node can complete a fleet proof.
`CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet` is the default, so a fleet of one node requests the
fleet posture and does not get it.

A node recruits up to two followers, so a fleet of three or more nodes holds
three copies of an acknowledged write. The ensemble keeps acknowledging while
one follower remains, therefore a fleet does not fall back to the bucket each
time it loses a follower.

A node without an ensemble stays correct. It acknowledges each write on a
bucket proof instead, so celld still does not acknowledge a write before a
durability proof covers it. The cost is latency: the write waits for the object
store, and an object store round trip is much slower than a follower fsync.

### The takeover recovery gate

The default fleet mode can acknowledge a write once the node-log
ensemble stores it; the bucket upload can complete later. Each process
session therefore creates a conditional node-log record before its
first fleet-durable acknowledgement.

A cold activation checks the prior owner's log records before it reads
the bucket. An absent record proves that the session never acknowledged
past the bucket, and a sealed record proves that recovery completed. An
open or recovering record makes the activation run recovery: it fences
the record with a compare-and-swap, seals the reachable followers,
uploads their retained segments and bundles into the per-cell prefixes,
and then marks the record sealed. The activation cannot restore until
this sequence completes.

### Full-prefix restore

A restore selects the newest epoch prefix that contains LTX data, and
it reads the full contiguous chain from transaction zero. celld no
longer writes an epoch seal object, and a legacy `e<epoch>.seal.json`
object does not limit the chain.

A fenced node can append an unacknowledged tail to an older prefix, and
a later restore can expose that tail. This does not violate the
contract, because a failed or absent acknowledgement does not prove
that the write is absent. The rule reads the full chain because a
node-log recovery or a bundle drain can add an acknowledged tail after
an earlier restore; a restore that stopped at the earlier cut would
hide that tail and lose acknowledged data.

### Self-fencing

Each node holds a lease in the bucket. The lease carries an expiry, and
the node renews it after one third of the lifetime (`CELLD_TTL_MS`,
default 10000 ms). A renewal that does not reach the bucket does not
fence the node, because the node retries while the published expiry has
not passed.

A node that cannot reach the bucket cannot renew and cannot replicate,
so it must not own cells. When its published expiry passes, it fences
itself: it stops each active cell, and it fails every request that it
has not completed. A node whose lease record another writer replaced or
removed fences at once, because that record proves the authority moved.

The fence writes nothing to the bucket. Each peer already reads the
lease as dead or replaced, so a peer can acquire the cells through the
ownership records. And a request is safe even before the fence runs,
because celld compares the current time against the published expiry
each time it routes a request.

A fenced node logs a line that starts with `SELF-FENCE:` and stops with
the exit code 3. celld reports other internal failures with the same
prefix and code, so the line names the cause. The fenced state is
terminal: only a restart returns the node to the fleet, through the
same cold-activation path that a peer failure uses.

The failure of a node is a normal input, not a recovery procedure; the
[testing page](testing.md) shows the kill tests that exercise this
path.

1: # Testing
2: 
3: celld makes three important promises:
4: 
5: - An acknowledged write is durable.
6: - A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
7: - Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
8:   same on celld.
9: 
10: We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
11: clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
12: Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
13: exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
14: deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
15: on live fleets.
16: 
17: ## Conformance: two runtimes, one output
18: 
19: We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
20: Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
21: Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
22: The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
23: is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
24: contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
25: runtime by accident.
26: 
27: The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
28: for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
29: engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
30: Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
31: Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
32: `celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
33: WebSockets, and lifecycle.
34: 
35: ## Specification: exhaustive at small size
36: 
37: The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
38: the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
39: four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
40: fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

# Testing

celld makes three important promises:

- An acknowledged write is durable.
- A cell has one writer at a time. It never has two.
- Code written for Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects operates the
  same on celld.

We try to break each promise at the layer where a failure shows most
clearly. We test the API contract with differential execution against the
Cloudflare runtime. We check the coordination protocol against an
exhaustively model-checked specification, and we test it with
deterministic simulation. We test the full system with fault injection
on live fleets.

## Conformance: two runtimes, one output

We test the compatibility promise differentially. We run each Workers and
Durable Objects program twice: once on workerd, the runtime binary that
Cloudflare operates in production, and once on celld, on identical bytes.
The two outputs must be equal. This shows two facts at once: the program
is real Cloudflare code, because workerd accepts it, and celld obeys the
contract, because the outputs are equal. A test cannot agree with our own
runtime by accident.

The corpus only grows. When celld gets a new API surface, we add fixtures
for that surface, and the fixtures must give equal output on the two
engines. We also port test suites from workerd itself: the Durable
Objects contract, the web-platform globals, and the upstream Web Platform
Tests. Before a release, we also replay scenarios through the full
`celld` binary in each deployment mode: storage, SQL, alarms, streams,
WebSockets, and lifecycle.

## Specification: exhaustive at small size

The coordination protocol is also specified in TLA+. Heyang Zhou wrote
the specifications against celld v0.1.0, and his model checking found
four bugs and a split-brain that lost an acknowledged write. All are
fixed. None had surfaced in our own review or testing.

Where simulation samples schedules, the checker enumerates them: at a
small configuration it visits every reachable state. The model grants
the implementation a linearizable object store and perfect shared
clocks, so a violation it finds needs no clock skew and no storage
anomaly to occur. The invariants are the first two promises at the top
of this page: one writer for each epoch, and no acknowledged write
lost. The fencing argument itself — that a stale owner's late writes
cannot cost an acknowledged write, because the epoch in the key keeps
its lineage apart — is checked, not asserted.

Every configuration carries a pinned expected verdict, and most of the
verdicts are failures: each failing configuration models a bug the
protocol once had, or a deliberately broken checker, and the model
must produce the counterexample. A configuration that stops failing
has lost its tooth. One tooth had already fallen out when the
specifications arrived; we repaired it.

Some specifications model a proposed protocol before it is built. When
the fence on write acknowledgments was redesigned, the design-stage
check produced an eight-state counterexample against the version it
replaced: a dormant cell resumes at its old epoch while its release is
in flight, acknowledges a write, and the takeover that follows
restores without it. The fix shipped; the counterexample stays as a
pinned failure.

The checker has also removed code: celld once sealed a cell's durable
history at restore, and the verdicts showed the seal defended only the
return of a write that was never acknowledged — an outcome celld does
not promise to prevent — while its permanent cut could turn a
recoverable ordering slip into a permanent loss. The seal is gone.

The specifications are a hand-synced snapshot, deliberately not in
continuous integration: a silently stale gate is worse than none. In
practice their updates have landed in the same changes that moved the
protocol, and a delta ledger records what the model does not yet
describe, including places where the model is weaker than the code
rather than wrong. Simulation remains the per-commit ratchet; the
model is its exhaustive small-configuration complement.

## Simulation: the protocol under adversarial schedules

The dangerous bugs live in the coordination: a crash during an ownership
handoff, a lease renewal that races a takeover, an alarm that fires
against a partially restored cell. These windows are nanoseconds wide and
open rarely, so a test cannot wait for them.

Thus the coordination protocol is a
[pure decision core](https://github.com/denoland/celld/tree/main/crates/logic)
with no I/O of its own: the clock, the randomness, and the object store
are interfaces, and a simulator drives the core. The simulated store
injects latency, compare-and-swap races, and lost responses; the clocks
drift apart; a node can crash at each await point. Scripted adversaries
play the cells: a handler that never returns, a write stream that stops
halfway. V8 stays out of the simulation, because V8 is not deterministic.

A seeded scheduler drives each run, so a failure is not a fluke: the seed
replays it exactly, every time, and we keep the seed until the bug is
dead. We examine each property for safety (two writers in one epoch, a
lost acknowledged write, an expired lease that comes back) and for
liveness (each armed alarm fires, and ownership settles on one node after
a crash). A property must survive tens of thousands of seeds, and the
core protocols have run through millions of different schedules.

Simulation has a known failure mode: the checker that cannot fail. So
we also test the checkers: we run deliberately broken variants of the
protocol against the properties, and the properties must find the damage.
A suite that stays green against a broken protocol is a broken suite.

## Live fleets: what simulation cannot see

Simulation cannot see the real S3 tail latency, the real kernel and
filesystem behavior, or V8 under memory pressure. The third layer is
therefore a permanent fleet lab: standard VMs from standard providers,
and a real bucket. The workloads rotate: chat rooms under many WebSocket
connections, working sets that shift across tens of thousands of cells
(each cell has a unique checksum), deployment cutovers under load, and
runs that fill the nodes to the memory limit. The lab qualifies each
release, and between releases it pushes the density and the fault
coverage further. Each run makes an archived evidence bundle: the
configuration, the verification sweeps, the node journals, the kernel
logs, and the phase timings. We keep a red run with the same care as a
green run, because a failure that the harness caught is a result, not a
retry.

We inject the faults between verification passes. A pass fetches each
cell through different nodes and compares the durable state exactly: the
status, the body, and the full message ledger. Each run therefore has a
clean picture before the fault and after it. A cell can be unavailable
for a short time while its ownership moves, but its committed state must
stay complete, and a live node must serve that state again.

The scenarios attack every seam that we know:

- Stop a node with `SIGKILL` in the middle of a write stream and delete
  its local database, so recovery can only come from the bucket. Every
  acknowledged write comes back, because the output gate held each
  response until the write was durable.
- Freeze an owner node, write to its cells through other nodes, and
  unfreeze it. The node sees that its lease moved and refuses to serve
  the old state, and each write from the other nodes lands exactly one
  time: one epoch has at most one writer.
- Cut a node off from the bucket. It fences itself, because a node that
  cannot replicate must not own cells.
- Throttle the bucket, so it answers each request with a 429. The engine
  slows to the write rate of the store and does not amplify the
  throttle, because a node that knows its replicated position does not
  ask a slow store for extra listings.
- Stop a full host at the provider level in the middle of a workload.
  Its cells move to the other nodes, and the returning host joins again
  with no duplicate residency.

Across every run of every scenario, no acknowledged write was lost and
no committed state was damaged; the verification sweeps show zero body
faults, zero status faults, and zero lost messages.

## A few numbers we trust

Each number includes the condition of its measurement. A number without
its conditions has no value.

- **The epoch fence holds under contention.** Five hundred claimants
  tried at the same time to own the same cells: 5,500 attempts, one
  writer for each epoch, zero violations.
- **A warm resident request is local.** A request to a resident cell does
  zero bucket operations and returns in p50 ~1.1 ms and p99 ~7 ms (a
  fixed-host measurement). Only a cold activation touches object storage.
- **A durable write waits for a durability proof.** A single node proves
  each write through the bucket, so one storage round trip is the minimum
  latency for that write. A fleet of two or more nodes can prove a write
  when each follower holds it on disk, and a follower fsync is much
  faster than a storage round trip: a lab fleet measured about 600 ms for
  a bucket proof and about 25 ms for a fleet proof. The bucket upload
  races every fleet proof and either one proves the write, so a slow
  follower cannot make a write slower than a bucket proof. Concurrent
  writes to one cell join one shared upload, so the throughput of one
  cell is not one round trip for each write.
- **A restore is normal work.** Placement handles the restore of an
  inactive cell as ordinary work, and not as an emergency procedure. The
  measured restore times come from the retired external replicator, so this
  page gives no number until a fleet run measures `celld-ltx`.
- **Ten small nodes held real scale.** A fleet of ten nodes, each with 4
  vCPU and 8 GB, held 10,000 resident cells and 20,000 concurrent
  WebSocket connections. We stopped two of the ten nodes, and the data of
  every cell was available again on another node in ~11 s at the tail
  (with reserve headroom).

## The failure edges we intend to find

We must also know where a policy stops, so we record the edges instead of
tuning them away. The clearest edge is the reserve headroom: a fleet that
is full to its resident limit has no space for the cells of a lost node,
so a failure of more than one node at the limit degrades the service,
and a fleet with headroom does not. We measure both sides of that line,
the good restoration with reserve and the red case without, because this
measurement is part of the work.

If you find an edge that we did not find, tell us: a schedule that breaks
a promise, a fault that we did not inject, a number that you cannot
reproduce. That is exactly the bug report that we want:
[github.com/denoland/celld/issues](https://github.com/denoland/celld/issues).

display.text:
# Telemetry

celld can record traces and logs for the requests it serves. The
feature is off by default, and the off state costs nothing. Set
`CELLD_OTEL=1` to turn it on.

The default sink is the fleet bucket. celld writes Parquet files under
the `telemetry/` prefix, so a fleet with a bucket has observability
with no other service. DuckDB can query these files directly. An
alternative sink sends the same data to an OpenTelemetry collector.

The schema is version `v0-unstable`. The column names can change
before a stable release, and each file carries the schema version in
its object metadata.

## Configuration

| variable | default | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CELLD_OTEL` | `0` | Set this value to `1` to enable telemetry. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_SINK` | `bucket` | `bucket` writes Parquet to the fleet bucket. `otlp` sends OTLP/HTTP protobuf to a collector instead. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_BUCKET` | the fleet bucket | A different bucket for the Parquet files, on the same endpoint and credentials. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_RETENTION` | `30d` | celld deletes telemetry files older than this. `none` disables the deletion, so your own lifecycle rules can control the data. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_MS` | `300000` | celld writes a Parquet file after this many milliseconds of buffered events. |
| `CELLD_OTEL_FLUSH_BYTES` | `5242880` | celld writes a Parquet file after the buffered events reach this many bytes. celld uses the limit it reaches first. |
| `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` | `parentbased_always_on` | A standard sampler name. `traceidratio` with `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` records a fraction of the traces. |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | `http://localhost:4318` | The collector base URL, for the `otlp` sink. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` also apply. |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `celld` | The service name in the exported resource. |

The `bucket` sink requires the node to have a fleet bucket
(`CELLD_BUCKET`). The `otlp` sink works on a node without one.

## What celld records

celld records a span for each request a stateless Worker serves, for
each event a cell serves (a fetch, an alarm, an RPC, a WebSocket
message), for each outbound `fetch()`, and for each cell start. A
span carries the request id, the cell, the isolate, the
queue wait, the outbound URL and status, and the durability facts the
runtime already knows.

celld also records each `console.log` line as a log record. The log
record carries the trace id and the span id of the handler that wrote
it, so a query can join the logs to the traces. The correlation
survives `await`.

celld reads the W3C `traceparent` header on incoming requests, so its
spans join the trace of the system in front of it. celld sends a
`traceparent` header on outbound `fetch()`, so downstream systems can
join too. A Worker call to a Durable Object stays in one trace.

I now have a thorough understanding of the repository. Let me map the key systems and design the wiki taxonomyaks, then submit the plan.

The repository is **celld** — a self-hosted, distributed Durable Objects runtime. Three crates:
- `crates/logic` — the clean-sheet decision core (pure state machine, `on_event`, Event/Effect, State)
- `crates/celld` — the effect executor / V8 shell adapter host
- `crates/ltx` — streaming SQLite replication (LTX format, port of Litestream)

Let me design the wiki taxonomy around meaningful systems.

3: //! The output gate: one choke point every egress passes through.
4: //!
5: //! # The rule
6: //!
7: //! Nothing that reveals a cell's state may leave this process while that cell
8: //! has a write it cannot prove durable. A client told about a write that a
9: //! crash then discards has been told something false, and no later message can
10: //! retract a side effect that has already left.
11: //!
12: //! # The implementation contract
13: //!
14: //! [`Channel`] enumerates every route that can reveal a cell's state. The shell
15: //! holds each effect and sends an [`Event::Output`] with its route. This module
16: //! applies one durability rule to every route and returns the same route in an
17: //! [`Effect::Release`].
18: //!
19: //! Each part of that contract has one implementation counterpart:
20: //!
21: //! | contract | implementation |
22: //! | --- | --- |
23: //! | enumerate every output route | the [`Channel`] enum |
24: //! | apply one rule to every route | the `channel` argument to [`State::output`] |
25: //! | bypass the gate when disabled | with `CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE=0`, the shell sends no [`Event::Output`] |
26: //! | release only revealable state | the output's barrier, or the barrier it trails, has settled |
27: //! | let the held effect leave | [`Effect::Release`] with `Ok` |
28: //!
29: //! **The core does not read the channel.** It stores what the shell gave it and
30: //! hands the same value back. A `match` on [`Channel`] inside this module would
31: //! split the invariant into six independent rules. Per-channel code belongs in
32: //! the shell and is limited to how an effect is held and how it is released.
33: //!
34: //! # Why one choke point
35: //!
36: //! Earlier implementations split this rule between a core reader gate, a shell
37: //! WebSocket queue, and an in-handler position check. Each mechanism had a
38: //! different view of the outstanding writes, so one channel could miss a write
39: //! that another mechanism knew about. One core barrier map gives every channel
40: //! the same view.
41: //!
42: //! # The second way a barrier opens
43: //!
44: //! Every channel passes through [`State::output`]. Not every barrier is opened
45: //! by one: `alarm_finished` opens its own when a firing's consuming commit is
46: //! unproven, owned by [`GateOwner::Alarm`] rather than by an output. An alarm
47: //! is not a seventh channel -- it settles by replay into the core, not by
48: //! release to the shell, so a [`Channel`] variant could not carry it -- but its
49: //! barrier lives in the same per-cell map, which is what matters here: a
50: //! read-only output trails the newest barrier on its cell without asking who
51: //! opened it, so it trails an alarm's unproven write exactly as it trails a
52: //! request's.
53: //!
54: //! An earlier alarm path proved its write inside [`Effect::FireAlarm`] without
55: //! registering a core barrier. A read-only output could therefore miss that
56: //! unproven write. The alarm now opens a barrier in the same map, so every
57: //! reader observes it.
58: //!
59: //! # Boundary
60: //!
61: //! A response body that streams is gated once, when the response is released.
62: //! Later chunks do not pass again. The model treats a response as atomic, so it
63: //! does not see this either.
64: 
65: use crate::*;
